messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Youssef Khalil is a 78-year-old Lebanese-American environmental scientist, married for over fifty years, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 70 following an incident that occurred approximately fourteen months ago in which he accidentally caused serious injury to another person. He was referred by his internist after his wife urged him to seek help, concerned by changes she had observed in him that she could no longer attribute to ordinary aging or fatigue.

The incident took place during what had been, by all accounts, a gentle afternoon. Youssef had been helping his youngest grandchild with a project in his home workshop — the kind of quiet, purposeful time he had always treasured in retirement. His granddaughter, eight years old, had wandered close while he was operating a piece of equipment he had used hundreds of times without incident. In a moment he still cannot reconstruct with any coherence, the machine caught her hand. The sound he heard in the seconds that followed — her sharp intake of breath, then the sustained, labored breathing of a child in shock — filled the room before the screaming began. Youssef himself has said almost nothing about what he saw. In sessions, he reaches for language and finds none; he opens his mouth, shakes his head slowly, and looks at his hands. What happened is present in him, he conveys, but sealed behind a wall he cannot climb. He has described the memory as feeling less like something that occurred in his life and more like footage from a catastrophe that happened to someone else — and yet, in the same breath, he will say that when it surfaces, it arrives not as recollection but as recurrence, immediate and total, as though the workshop is still around him and his granddaughter is still in front of him.

In the months following the injury, Youssef's daily life reorganized itself around a set of experiences he had not anticipated and could not explain. He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that feeling at ease was a form of negligence — that the accident had happened precisely because he had been comfortable, unhurried, happy. Moments of relaxation now arrive with a physical unease he cannot override. When, on a warm evening, he finds himself momentarily content sitting on the porch, something tightens in his chest and he goes inside. He had been a man who laughed easily; he had come to distrust that ease entirely. His wife has noticed that he stiffens when she reaches for him — when she puts her arms around him in the way she has for decades, he does not pull away, but he does not return it, and she has stopped initiating as often. He knows she is hurt by this and he has no words to offer her that feel adequate or true.

His professional life, though nominally retired, still involves occasional consultations with a university research group studying wetland restoration. During a site visit last spring, a graduate student standing behind him stumbled on uneven ground and grabbed his arm to steady herself, breathing hard from the exertion of the walk. The sound of her labored breath stopped him completely. He stood still for several seconds while the group moved ahead, and later told his wife only that he had felt unwell. He has not returned to the field since, citing his age, though the work had previously given him considerable satisfaction.

What finally brought Youssef to seek help was a moment at his granddaughter's birthday celebration three months ago. She had recovered well, and she hugged him when he arrived — unselfconsciously, with her full small weight — and he stood in that embrace feeling nothing he recognized as love, only the sound of her breathing against his shoulder, and the absolute, disorienting conviction that the afternoon in the workshop was happening again, right then, in the middle of the party. He left early. He has said he does not want to lose what remains of the time he has with his family. What frightens him most is that he already feels he has.
